extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator; educated London public interested in manners, letter-writing, conversation, and devotional/public reading
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical moral essays offering advice on social behaviour, letter-writing, aesthetic judgment, and public reading; combines prescriptive rules and illustrative examples for conduct in company, love-letters, and liturgical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good love-letter
rubrics_metrics.description: A love-letter should combine 'the Advantages of a liberal Education, some Knowledge, and as much Contempt of the World, join'd with the Endeavours towards a Life of strict Virtue and Religion' and express 'dis-interested Passion' and constancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sincere and elevated in sentiment; raise new ideas in a well-disposed reader's breast; show steady devotion over time (constancy even after many years of marriage); brevity from haste is excusable but the sentiment must be genuine. (Examples: phrases like 'Your most Obedient, most Devoted Servant' and apologies for hurried writing are acceptable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not burden company with private complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal cares, distresses, diseases, uneasinesses, and dislikes of our own 'are by no means to be obtruded upon our Friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in social company you should contribute good humour and cheerfulness rather than recount private melancholy; those constantly complaining (valetudinarians) should be dissuaded from speaking of themselves in company. If the room is merry, one should not sour it by airing personal woes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation as an indulgence requiring good-will
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation is an indulgence to the sociable part of our make and should incline us to bring our proportion of good will or good humour among the friends we meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat social meetings as requiring an attitude of cheerfulness and moderation; avoid being a drain on others' spirits and aim to preserve the 'chearfulness of our Spirits' in company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain equality of mind (moderation of passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To enjoy life and health as a constant feast, one should 'arrive at an Equality of Mind' and not be overly elated by good fortune nor dejected by misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate steady temper: neither extravagant joy nor excessive sorrow; practice moderate cares, exercise the body and keep the mind at ease. Aim for a sobriety of heart that is 'above all Pleasures' and less susceptible to Fortune's vicissitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical perspective on death and future life
rubrics_metrics.description: A contemplative view of death and hope in another life lessens fear of present ills and supports cheerfulness: 'Let us be Adventurers for another World' and view death as a possible gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting a conviction or hopeful speculation about an afterlife is offered as a practical way to sustain tranquillity and to render pain and decline less disturbing; this is both ethical counsel and a method for maintaining cheerfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the deceptive power of beauty (for observers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty exerts an 'irresistible' prepossession: 'a graceful Person is a more powerful Recommendation than the best Letter' and 'a short liv'd Tyranny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate judgment to resist being unduly influenced by physical beauty; remember beauty is a gift of nature (not a moral perfection) and ephemeral. Attend to character and virtue rather than being captivated by outward form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to the beautiful: prefer natural simplicity to affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural simplicity of aspect is praised over artful patience to be stared at; affectation spoils excellence ('Affectation prevents her Excellencies from walking together').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those possessing beauty should avoid theatrical or affected behaviour (contrived looks, posed carelessness) because artifice undermines the genuine charms of nature; modest, unforced manners preserve attractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining wit and beauty as an affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman who displays both wit and contrived beauty may appear to be neither: 'tho' a Wit and Beauty, is allowed to be neither, because she will always be both.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow virtues to cohere naturally rather than showcasing them in a manner that defeats their effect; wit used to display beauty (or vice versa) is an anti-pattern that diminishes both qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware apparent innocence masking vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms of beauty are deceptive: one may present an aspect 'as Innocent as the famed Lucrece, but a Mind as Wild as Cleopatra' (Omnamante's type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution toward outward innocence: look for consistent behaviour and moral character rather than taking a harmless countenance at face value; be aware of manipulation through affectation (tears, tremors used to disarm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and authority are not proved by wagers/wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of young men who 'wager themselves into Statesmen, Historians, Geographers, Mathematicians'—using money to assume intellectual authority is a false method to wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept claims to knowledge that rest on the ability to stake money; true learning is shown by reading and understanding, not by betting or by the strength of one's purse. Wagering is an anti-pattern for establishing intellectual credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful use of public spaces (no disruptive whistling/singing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who 'sing Opera-Tunes or Whistle in a full House' are admonished: they have 'no Right to act here as if he were in an empty Room.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the shared nature of public rooms: avoid making noises that interrupt others' lawful discourse. The writer proposes 'divide the Spaces of a Publick Room' and that whistlers/singers be restrained by common decency or law/equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good reading of the Common Prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Common Prayer should be read 'so distinctly, so emphatically, and so fervently' that it holds attention and moves the congregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a model reader as an example; read with clearness, loudness, and strength; maintain evenness of voice and delivery; avoid 'Pindarick Readers' who alternate wildly in pace and tone; avoid reading so fast as to be impatient, and avoid indifferent, lifeless reading that suggests not understanding the language. Use proper emphasis and vary voice according to sentence nature to read movingly and fervently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cant and affected tones in public devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cant signifies 'sudden Exclamations, Whinings, unusual Tones, and in fine all Praying and Preaching, like the unlearned of the Presbyterians.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt whining, artificial, or exaggerated tones in reading or prayer to avoid the charge of cant; the aim is reverent, intelligible, and measured delivery rather than theatrical or unintelligible affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper physical and behavioral posture for reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers who affect a 'rakish negligent Air by folding their Arms, and lolling on their Book' display indecency and poor example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain decent behaviour and a comely erection of body while reading; posture and demeanor influence the efficacy of public reading and teach others appropriate deportment.
